modern: This is a fine saying of Plato: that he who is speaking about men should also look at earthly things as if he were viewing them from some higher place; he should look at them in their assemblies, armies, farm labours, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, the noise of the law courts, desert places, various nations of barbarians, feasts, lamentations, markets, a mixture of all things and an orderly combination of opposites.
original: This is a fine saying of Plato: That he who is discoursing about men should look also at earthly things as if he viewed them from some higher place; should look at them in their assemblies, armies, agricultural labors, marriages, treaties, births, deaths, noise of the courts of justice, desert places, various nations of barbarians, feasts, lamentations, markets, a mixture of all things and an orderly combination of contraries.

explained.summary:
Marcus quotes a saying he credits to Plato: when you talk about human beings, look at them as if from high above. See their assemblies, armies, farming, weddings, treaties, births and deaths, lawsuits, deserts, foreign peoples, feasts, funerals and markets all at once.

From up there, life looks like a great mixture, yet an ordered combination of opposites. The view from above cools your judgement and reveals the pattern.
explained.today: Picture your town from a plane window: the school run, a wedding, a hospital ward, a football match, a funeral, all happening at once. Your own worry is one dot in that busy, oddly coherent scene.
